quick: Intubation: 0.15-0.2 mg/kg IV bolus; maintenance infusion ~1-3 mcg/kg/min (titrate to nerve stimulator)
Use only if clearly needed; monitor neonate for neuromuscular effects if used near delivery
Single peri-operative use unlikely to affect a breastfed infant; limited data
Organ-independent (Hofmann) elimination - no major adjustment in renal failure
Organ-independent elimination - no major adjustment in hepatic failure
Peripheral nerve stimulator (train-of-four), ventilation, depth of anesthesia
summary: Cisatracurium besylate is an intermediate-acting nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker used as an adjunct to general anesthesia to facilitate tracheal intubation and to provide skeletal muscle relaxation during surgery or mechanical ventilation in the ICU. It competitively blocks acetylcholine at the motor end-plate and is eliminated largely by organ-independent Hofmann degradation, making it useful in renal and hepatic failure. It produces no analgesia or sedation, so adequate anesthesia is essential, and it requires mechanical ventilation and nerve-stimulator monitoring.
indications: Adjunct to general anesthesia to facilitate tracheal intubation (adults and pediatric patients 1 month to 12 years)
Skeletal muscle relaxation during surgery (adults and pediatric patients 2 to 12 years, bolus or infusion)
Skeletal muscle relaxation for mechanical ventilation in the ICU (adults)

dosage.n: Onset of good intubating conditions ~1.5-2 min at higher dose; not for rapid-sequence intubation

dosage.d: Bolus 0.03 mg/kg as needed, or infusion approximately 1 to 3 mcg/kg/min
dosage.n: Titrate to peripheral nerve stimulator response

dosage.d: Infusion titrated to effect (commonly ~3 mcg/kg/min initial, adjust)
dosage.n: Monitor train-of-four; limit toxic metabolite exposure
Avoid benzyl-alcohol-preserved multidose vials in infants <1 month

admin: Administer intravenously only, by or under the supervision of clinicians experienced with neuromuscular blockers and their complications
Use only where personnel and equipment for intubation, mechanical ventilation, oxygen, and resuscitation are immediately available - the patient must be ventilated
Use a peripheral nerve stimulator (train-of-four) to monitor blockade depth, guide dosing, and assess recovery
Ensure adequate sedation/general anesthesia first - cisatracurium provides no analgesia, sedation, or amnesia
moa: Cisatracurium is the R-cis,R-cis isomer of atracurium. It binds competitively to nicotinic cholinergic (acetylcholine) receptors on the motor end-plate, antagonizing the action of acetylcholine and blocking neuromuscular transmission to produce flaccid skeletal muscle paralysis. This nondepolarizing block is reversible by acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as neostigmine. It is eliminated chiefly by Hofmann elimination (pH- and temperature-dependent spontaneous chemical degradation), independent of hepatic or renal function.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to cisatracurium (severe anaphylactic reactions reported)
Use of the 10 mL multiple-dose (benzyl-alcohol-containing) vials in neonates <1 month and low-birth-weight infants
relative: Neuromuscular diseases (myasthenia gravis, Eaton-Lambert) - exaggerated and prolonged block; reduce dose
Severe electrolyte disturbance or acid-base abnormality

preg: There are limited data. Use cisatracurium during pregnancy only if clearly needed. When used near delivery, monitor the neonate for residual neuromuscular blockade.
lact: It is not known whether cisatracurium is excreted in human milk. Given its short duration and single peri-operative use, clinically significant exposure to a breastfed infant is unlikely.
renal: Because cisatracurium is eliminated predominantly by organ-independent Hofmann degradation, no major dose adjustment is needed in renal impairment, including end-stage renal disease. Onset may be slightly slower.
hepatic: Hofmann elimination is independent of hepatic function, so no major dose adjustment is required in hepatic impairment.

major: Other neuromuscular blockers (additive/synergistic block; cross-reactive anaphylaxis risk)
moderate: Volatile anesthetics (isoflurane, sevoflurane, enflurane) - potentiate and prolong block
Aminoglycoside, polymyxin, clindamycin, and other antibiotics that impair neuromuscular transmission
minor: Chronic phenytoin or carbamazepine (may shorten duration / cause resistance)
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor with peripheral nerve stimulation rather than laboratory tests

serious: Anaphylaxis / severe hypersensitivity (cross-reactive with other neuromuscular blockers)
Inadequate paralysis reversal leading to respiratory failure
Seizures (laudanosine metabolite accumulation with prolonged ICU infusion)
rare: Myopathy/prolonged weakness after long-term ICU use (especially with corticosteroids)
emergency: Apnea/respiratory failure from residual paralysis or accidental administration

monitoring: Peripheral nerve stimulator (train-of-four) to titrate dosing and assess recovery
Continuous ventilation, oxygenation, and end-tidal CO2
For prolonged ICU infusion: signs of residual weakness/myopathy and metabolite-related effects
counsel: This is a paralytic given only in the operating room or ICU by anesthesia/critical-care teams
It does not cause sleep or relieve pain - it is always given with anesthesia or sedation
Breathing must be supported by a ventilator while it is in effect
Tell your anesthesiologist about any prior reaction to muscle relaxants or anesthesia
Recovery of muscle strength is monitored before the breathing tube is removed
pk: Maximum block in about 2-3 minutes (faster with higher bolus, ~1.5 min at 0.2 mg/kg)
Peak neuromuscular block within a few minutes of an IV bolus
Clinically effective block about 30-60 minutes (intermediate-acting), dose dependent
Refrigerate at 2-8 C; protect from light; do not freeze
pearls: Eliminated by organ-independent Hofmann degradation - the relaxant of choice in combined hepatic and renal failure
Causes minimal histamine release compared with atracurium, so it is hemodynamically stable
NOT suitable for rapid-sequence intubation because of its onset time
No analgesia or sedation - inadequate anesthesia can leave a paralyzed but aware patient
Prolonged ICU infusion can accumulate the metabolite laudanosine (CNS excitation/seizure risk in animals); avoid the benzyl-alcohol multidose vial in neonates
missed: Cisatracurium is titrated by clinicians as a bolus or continuous infusion during anesthesia or ICU ventilation, so the concept of a patient-missed dose does not apply. Dosing is guided by neuromuscular monitoring.
overdose: Overdose causes prolonged, profound neuromuscular blockade and apnea. Management: maintain a patent airway and controlled mechanical ventilation with adequate sedation until spontaneous recovery is adequate; an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (e.g. neostigmine with an anticholinergic) can antagonize the block once recovery has begun, guided by a nerve stimulator. Support cardiovascular function as needed.
